results.blind_working: The radial leads point at O, so they give no field there. For the arc, B = (μ0·I/4πR)·θ with θ = 3π/2, giving B = 3μ0·I/(8R).
On the axis, B = B0·R³/(R²+x²)^(3/2). With x = √3R this is B0·R³/(2R)³ = B0/8 = 40/8 = 5 μT.
The two arcs are in parallel, so I1·R1 = I2·R2. Resistance is proportional to θ, so I1·θ1 = I2·θ2. The arc fields are equal and opposite, making the net field zero. So A is false and R is true.
Rewinding into two turns halves the radius and doubles N. Since B ∝ N/R, B becomes 4 times larger, so I is correct. For a point on the element's own line, dl × r = 0, so dB = 0; II is correct.
Inside the wire, B = μ0Ir/(2πR²). At r = 1 cm, R = 2 cm this is μ0I/(2π)×25. Outside, B = μ0I/(2πr); at r = 4 cm this is μ0I/(2π)×25. So B1/B2 = 1.
n = 500/0.5 = 1000 per m. Field at the centre = μ0nI = 2.51×10^-3 T. At the end the field is half of this, 1.26×10^-3 T.
Outside a straight wire B ∝ 1/r (A-III). Inside a solid wire B ∝ r (B-II). Inside a hollow pipe no current is enclosed, so B = 0 (C-I). Inside a solenoid B = μ0nI (D-IV).

A is true: the line integral depends only on enclosed current. B is true. C is true. D is false: doubling length halves n, so the field halves. E is false: the field is zero on the axis. Correct set is A, B, C.
The magnetic force qv×B is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work. Speed and kinetic energy stay constant, while the direction of velocity (and momentum) changes.
From qV = p²/2m, p = √(2mqV). Then r = p/(qB) = √(2mV/q)/B, so r ∝ √(m/q). For the proton m/q = 1; for the alpha particle m/q = 4/2 = 2. So r_p : r_α = 1 : √2.
The radius is r = v sin60°/ω = 3 cm. The pitch is p = v cos60° · 2π/ω = 2πr·cot60° = 2π·3/√3 = 2√3π cm.
The undeflected condition qE = qvB gives v = E/B, which is independent of q and m. So the selector picks a speed, not a charge-to-mass ratio. A is false and R is true.
The period T = 2πm/(qB) does not depend on speed, so Statement I is false. The proton and electron have opposite charges, so they circulate in opposite senses; Statement II is false.
Weight mg = 0.02 × 10 = 0.2 N. Set BIL = mg, so I = 0.2 / (0.4 × 0.5) = 1 A
Effective length is the diameter 2R = 0.2 m, so F = BI(2R) = 0.5 × 5 × 0.2 = 0.5 N
A: perpendicular wire gives BIl. B: sin30° gives BIl/2. C: semicircle acts as its diameter, giving 2BIR. D: closed loop gives zero. So A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I
A is true. B is false because the force is maximum when the wire is perpendicular to the field. C is true. D is false because the first finger points along the field. E is true. So A, C and E
F/L = μ0·I1·I2/(2πd) = 2×10⁻⁷ × 5 × 8 / 0.2 = 4×10⁻⁵ N/m. Currents in the same direction attract.
Opposite currents repel, so the upward magnetic force balances Q's weight. 2×10⁻⁷ × 50 × 20 / d = 0.002 × 10 = 0.02 N/m, so d = 2×10⁻⁴ / 0.02 = 0.01 m = 1 cm.
F/L ∝ I1·I2/d. New force = (2 × 3 / 2) F = 3F.
A is true because the forces form a Newton's third-law pair. R is true, but attraction does not explain why the magnitudes are equal.

I (reading 'parallel current' as same direction): the upward attraction must not exceed λg, and raising the fixed wire weakens the force, so I is correct. II: F/L = 2×10⁻⁷ × 2 × 2 / 1 = 8×10⁻⁷ N/m, not 4×10⁻⁷, so II is incorrect.
The plane is parallel to B, so the normal is at 90° to B. τ = NIAB = 50×2×4×10⁻³×0.5 = 0.2 N m.
For wire length L, the circle has area L²/(4π) and the square has area L²/16. Maximum torque is proportional to area, so the ratio is (L²/(4π))/(L²/16) = 4/π.
Parallel: τ = 0, U = −mB. Antiparallel: τ = 0, U = +mB. Plane parallel to B (θ = 90°): τ = mB, U = 0. θ = 60°: τ = (√3/2)mB, U = −mB/2.

A is true: net force in a uniform field is zero. B is true: the formula holds for any planar shape. C is false: torque is maximum when the plane is parallel to B. D is true: the antiparallel position is an unstable equilibrium. E is false: U is minimum when the plane is perpendicular to B.
In a radial field the plane of the coil stays parallel to B at every position. So the torque is NIAB, which is balanced by kθ. This gives θ = (NAB/k)·I, so deflection is proportional to current.
S = Ig·G/(I − Ig) = 0.01×99/0.99 = 1 Ω. The shunt is connected in parallel.
R = V/Ig − G = 10/0.005 − 40 = 2000 − 40 = 1960 Ω. The resistance is connected in series.
The soft iron core concentrates the field and raises B. Current sensitivity is NAB/k, so it increases with B. Both statements are true and R explains A.

I: Doubling N with the same wire doubles the wire length, so R doubles. Voltage sensitivity NAB/(kR) is therefore unchanged, so I is false. II: A parallel combination has resistance less than either resistor, so II is true.
μ = (e/2m_e)L in magnitude; it is antiparallel to L because the electron's charge is negative.
A: NIA → III. B: μ0·2m/(4πx^3) → IV. C: eh/(4πm_e) → II. D: evr/2 → I.
A true. B false: clockwise current gives a south pole. C true: e/2m_e ≈ 8.8e10 C/kg. D true. E false: the axial field varies as 1/x^3.
Field lines form closed loops. Outside the magnet they run N to S, so inside they run S to N.
A cut perpendicular to the axis keeps the pole strength at m = 5 A m and halves the length to 0.05 m. So M = 5 × 0.05 = 0.25 A m^2.
M = NIA = 200 × 2 × 5e-4 = 0.2 A m^2. Pole strength m = M/l = 0.2/0.04 = 5 A m.
By Gauss's law for magnetism, the net flux through any closed surface is zero, so A is false. Field lines are closed loops, so R is true.

A cut along the axis halves the cross-section, so both pole strength and moment are halved; Statement I is wrong. Fields superpose into a single net field, so field lines never intersect; Statement II is wrong.
For a short magnet, B_axial = (μ0/4π)·2m/r³ and B_eq = (μ0/4π)·m/r³, so the ratio is 2:1.
A = 2m/r³ → II. B = m/r³ → IV. C = 2m/(8r³) = m/4r³ → III. D = m/8r³ → I.
A true. B false: the equatorial field is opposite to m. C true: B ∝ 1/r³, so doubling r gives 1/8. D true: for r≫l the denominator becomes r⁴. E false: the field is minimum at θ=90°.
τ = mB sinθ = 2 × 0.5 × sin30° = 0.5 N m
T ∝ 1/√B; B becomes 9 times larger, so T becomes 3/3 = 1 s
U = −mB cosθ is maximum at θ = 180°, so antiparallel is unstable equilibrium; R correctly explains A
Net force in a uniform field is zero, so I is false. W(0→90°) = mB and W(0→180°) = 2mB, so II is true
Bismuth is the classic diamagnetic material. Aluminium and sodium are paramagnetic, and nickel is ferromagnetic.
The level falls because the liquid is repelled from the strong-field region, so it is diamagnetic. Water is diamagnetic. Liquid O2, CuCl2 solution and Al are paramagnetic.
Superconductor: chi = -1 (perfect diamagnet). Copper: small negative chi. Aluminium: small positive chi. Iron: chi >> 1.
A is true. B is false (mu_r < 1). C is true. D is false (it aligns parallel). E is true (diamagnetic chi is nearly independent of temperature). So A, C and E are correct.

Diamagnetic susceptibility arises from induced orbital moments, not from thermal alignment of permanent dipoles. So it is essentially independent of temperature. Paramagnetic and ferromagnetic susceptibilities both depend on temperature.
By Curie's law, χ ∝ 1/T. So χ = 3.0e-4 × 300/200 = 4.5e-4.
By the Curie-Weiss law, χ = C/(T − Tc). At 731 K, T − Tc = 100 K. Halving χ requires T − Tc = 200 K, so T = 831 K.
Above Tc, ferromagnets become paramagnetic, so A is true. Their susceptibility follows χ = C/(T − Tc) and still depends on temperature, so R is false.

Gadolinium has Tc ≈ 293 K, so at 330 K it is paramagnetic. Nickel has Tc = 631 K, so at 330 K it is ferromagnetic. Statement I is false. In a weak field M = C·B/T, so doubling both B and T leaves M unchanged. Statement II is true.
